title: Care Less: Beneficial Reasons to Loosen Your Grip at Work
content:
Care Less: Reasons to Loosen Your Grip at Work

Hot take, I’m about to encourage you to care less at work. In an industry where we pour our blood, sweat, and tears into every possible decision, the idea of encouraging designers to care less about their work might sound heretical. After all, isn’t pixel-perfection what we were hired for? While yes, that is absolutely true, I’ve been exploring the counterintuitive notion that designers can actually benefit from caring a little less about their work, especially when working in collaborative, fast-paced team environments.

1. Be a better steward for creativity and collaboration

Designing for businesses, by nature, thrive on collaboration. It’s the exchange of the team’s diverse ideas and perspectives that often lead to breakthroughs and innovative solutions. Designers who cling too tightly to their work can inadvertently stifle the creative synergy that emerges when minds come together. By easing up on the reins, designers create space for their colleagues to contribute, thus fostering an environment where the final product is enriched by multiple viewpoints.

2. Be one with the chaos

In dynamic work environments, change is inevitable. Teams often iterate rapidly, responding to feedback, market changes, and user needs (sometimes read as “stakeholder preferences”;) Designers who are willing to let go of their attachment to specific design elements can more effectively adapt to these changes. A certain level of detachment enables them to pivot quickly, experiment with new ideas, and embrace evolving project requirements with greater ease.

3. Foster constructive, healthy critique

Critique is an essential part of the design process. However, designers who are overly invested in their work might struggle to accept or benefits fully to constructive feedback. By taking a step back and not treating their designs as extensions of their identity, designers can open themselves up to more meaningful critique. This, in turn, results in iterative improvements and a more refined final product.

Bonus note: Find solutions which help you work faster, not work more.

I don’t know who needs to hear this but, use auto-layout, variables, dear god use components, work through building that easy-to-edit template for whatever ethereal social assets you’re going to need to produce time and again. Time committed and emotional attachment are directly correlated. I’d highly encourage investing time in building fast workflows. There’s no reason to be doing things by hand any more.

4. Encourage others’ growth, empowerment and delegation

Empowerment and delegation are cornerstones of effective teamwork. When designers are willing to relinquish some control over their designs, they not only empower their team members but also create opportunities for skill development and growth. Allowing others to contribute to their work can foster a sense of ownership and collaboration that propels the project forward. This statement is true for designers with less experience, but can also be opportunity to manage up.

5. Hedge Against Burnout and Enhance Well-being

I know so many folks who stay up late into the night working on…work. I’ve definitely been there. However, I believe there is a time and place in one’s career for that kind of dedication or long hours spent tweaking and trying things out. But, over a long career, this unrelenting commitment can lead to burnout, stress, and a compromised sense of well-being. Embracing a slightly less rigid approach to work can allow for us to strike a healthier work-life balance. By recognizing that not every design decision needs to be a life-or-death choice, designers can free themselves from the emotional and mental strains that come with excessive perfectionism.

In a field where passion and dedication run deep, it might seem counterintuitive to advocate for designers to care less about their work. However, by embracing a more balanced and adaptable approach, designers can unlock new dimensions of creativity, collaboration, and well-being. This is not an endorsement of mediocrity, but rather an acknowledgment that the pursuit of perfection can sometimes hinder the very progress we aim to achieve. Take a deep breath, trust the process and your team, and close your laptop before 7pm.
